## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: Tobias says guests want a real person who knows the house, while Chiara says the phones are already covered and her real burden is group requests and emails without rates, so these are two different points and leaving each on its own is how I would read them too.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and no group was formed, so nothing junk was let in.

founder.order_why: The flow moves the way I'd explain Codyco: who misses the calls and when, then what it costs, then how the AI answering fits the desk, then the pilot. Each step builds on the one before.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 have the same headline ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so they read as a repeat, split by the 7-day window on screen 4. Screens 12 and 13 show the compatibility check twice, and 16 and 17 show the relative-advantage check twice; the second pass felt like the same screen again.
founder.missing: Nothing asked who pays. The revenue or reservations director decides and the hotel's owner signs off, but every question was about the reservation agent. Nothing asked the price either: the €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel and the per-hotel monthly licence. 'Offer a pilot?' took a yes but not the fee. I also never got to put in my 5%-of-calls-missed figure as what the problem costs a hotel group.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks about forwarding unanswered calls on my last booking call right after the idea card, which breaks the flow from the missed-call moment into whether Codyco would help, and it reads like a screening question that belonged back in Part 1.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 5 both go back to a reservation call that rang out unanswered, the second time just to frame the Codyco question.
PRIMARY.missing: How many calls we actually miss on a peak shift like a trade-fair Saturday, what happens to those callers now (overflow to another hotel, voicemail, callback list), and whether guests calling in German or English with group or corporate bookings could be handled; nothing on pricing, PMS/CRS integration or handing over to a human agent.

screens.why1: Right after I typed how Codyco fits into the office's day, Keel shows me the reviewed conditions before I pick one to test, which is the obvious next step.

screens.why3: An agent knows whether a missed call rolled over to another number, but whether they were 'allowed' to let software write into the PMS is the IT team's or the director's call, so many agents would guess.
screens.why4: Two rows, distinct, within the 2 to 4 band and the 16-word limit, each one thing to weigh.
screens.why5: My row named OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo, and the review turned it into a generic 'outside software' permission, so the integrations I sell on are gone from the screen.
screens.why7: Forwarding as a permission is right and tests the step the whole mechanism rests on, but the PMS row is nearly settled for German hotel groups, since booking engines and channel managers already write bookings into the PMS, so it can hardly be refuted.
screens.instead: Keep 'Were allowed to have unanswered calls forwarded to another number' (suggested) and replace the PMS row with 'ran OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo as their PMS', the products I named.

screens.why1: After Keel reviewed my conditions, picking the one condition strangers get asked is the obvious next step before the solution's belief is fixed.
screens.why2: Call forwarding, the PMS and bookings written in from outside software are everyday words to me and to any reservations director in a German hotel group.
screens.why3: An agent knows whether unanswered calls roll over to another number, but whether they are 'allowed' is the GM's or the phone provider's call, so some would guess at the permission rather than the fact.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and both real for my mechanism, and Keel's suggestion has a sensible why, but the first row is capitalised and the second is not, which reads as one row pasted from somewhere else.
screens.why5: I typed 'could forward unanswered calls to another number', which is the phone system's ability; Keel turned it into 'were allowed to have ... forwarded', which moves it a little toward a permission I never framed.
screens.why7: The card's rules are met: a permission row with the bar on 'only with help or approval, or no', two rows with Keel's suggestion marked and given a why, and a belief that can go either way because many groups' phone setups do not forward to an outside number.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? -- Could have unanswered calls forwarded to another number · Were allowed to let outside software write bookings into the PMS (Keel's suggestion), same capitalisation on both.

screens.why1: Right after I told Keel how it fits with call forwarding and the PMS, asking what it does better than how the desk handles missed calls today is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: The question and the hint are plain; I knew straight away to write that booking calls that ring out get answered and turned into bookings.
screens.why3: It asks about my own product against how reservation offices handle missed calls today, which I know from the 7 groups we work with.
screens.why4: There is a typing box and one escape chip, and 'I'm not sure' is the right way out because it just leaves the dimension out.
screens.why5: Nothing is reworded on this screen; my two benefits stand in my own words, ready for the Check.
screens.why7: The box asks for what the card wants: 1 to 4 benefits, each up to 9 words, set against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape; the generic example 'less time on it each week' is not a benefit my agents would name, but it bends no rule.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Codyco does better, Keel shows the rows it drafted for me to check, which is exactly where this check belongs.
screens.why2: Missed calls, bookings and a busy desk are everyday words in a reservations office, though the belief's 'would have given them missed calls turned into bookings' reads a little stiffly.
screens.why3: Every agent knows the last booking call that rang out and whether it was ever won back, so the belief is about their own shift.
screens.why4: The second row only covers peak ('when the desk is busy') and drops the after-hours and holiday calls that are half my pitch, and it is close to being the means of the first row rather than its own gain.
screens.why5: My words are 'after hours, during peak hours, on holidays', and 'when the desk is busy' narrows that to the rush, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why7: The count, the word limit, the noun-phrase rows and the hard case (a call that rang out) all meet the card, and the belief carries both rows joined with 'and', but the two rows lean on one gain (answering is how the missed call becomes a booking), which bends the no-overlap rule.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Missed booking calls turned into bookings' · 'Every call answered, after hours, at peak and on holidays' -- belief: For most, with it, the last time a reservation call of theirs rang out would have given them that booking and an answer at any hour.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Codyco does better, Keel reads my benefit back with the belief it will test, which is the natural next step before strangers see the item.
screens.why2: The row is in my words, but the belief needs a second read: 'a reservation call of theirs rang out' is stilted, and 'would have given them missed calls turned into bookings' doesn't parse cleanly for a single call.
screens.why3: A reservation agent knows the call that rang out on their shift and whether it ended up as a booking, so the belief is about their own shift.
screens.why4: The one row is short, a noun phrase, mine, and the guidance (1 to 4) fits; nothing on the list is odd or overlapping.
screens.why5: 'Missed calls turned into bookings' is exactly my pitch (the 5% that ring out becoming paid bookings in the PMS), unchanged.
screens.why7: The hard case is rightly the moment it went wrong (the call that rang out), not any shift, and the belief carries my only row, but plugging a plural benefit into one rung-out call ('the last time a call rang out would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') bends the belief's sense against the single moment the stranger will be asked about.
screens.instead: Row: 'Missed calls turned into bookings' -- belief: 'For most, with it, the last booking call that rang out unanswered would have ended as a booking.'

screens.why1: After compatibility and relative advantage, asking what effort my reservation agents take to start using it is the obvious next step of the solution.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps and learning are plain words to me, and the hint's limits of four efforts and nine words are clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what my agents would do: let the missed calls go to the AI and pick up the ones it hands back to the desk.
screens.why4: My two rows are distinct efforts in their voice, base-form verbs under nine words, and the I'm not sure chip fits a founder who cannot name the effort.
screens.why5: The rows are my own words from the material, the handover and the hand-back, kept as I typed them.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the agents take themselves, one a hand-over and one the new habit of taking hand-backs, in their voice, neither Compatibility's forwarding nor Purchase friction's data review, and I'm not sure is the founder's escape.

screens.why1: After I typed what they'd have to do to start, it makes sense to check Keel's wording of those efforts before I pick one to test.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls, the AI and the desk are all words my agents use, and each row reads clearly on first pass.
screens.why3: Taking the calls the AI passes over is something an agent does every shift, but whether a group's missed calls get handed to the AI is usually decided by the director and set up by IT, so an agent would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but 'the desk' leaves out the central-office and call-center agents I'm actually selling to.
screens.why5: This is still my mechanism: missed calls go to the AI, and the AI sends the calls it can't handle back to the team.
screens.why7: Both rows use 'their', start with a verb, stay under 9 words, number two of the allowed 1 to 4, and lead to a belief that can go either way, but row 1 is close to the forwarding Compatibility already tested, and to the director's decision, rather than a step the agent takes.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Trust the AI with their missed booking calls' and 'Take every call the AI hands to the team', with the second picked to test, because that is the new habit each agent actually takes on.

screens.why1: Right after I listed and checked the efforts, picking the one most likely to stop my reservation agents is the obvious next step before the test is written.
screens.why2: Both rows are in my trade's plain words, missed booking calls and the desk, and the title and intro read on first pass.
screens.why3: I know my agents and which of these two they would push back on; letting the AI take their missed calls is the one I hear about on every demo.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one before use (letting go of the calls) and one in use (taking the handovers), both in 'their' voice; no third step is missing that I would add.
screens.why5: The rows and the belief are exactly the efforts I typed, and the picked row is served verbatim as the test.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the agent takes themselves, each one effort within 9 words, the founder's own and in order, neither a Compatibility or Purchase friction condition; the belief can go either way on the yes/only-if versus probably-not/no split, and the escape belongs to the stranger's item.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether to end it with a pilot ask, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is my own word, since my whole launch offer is a pilot, and the hint shows the exact line people will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect pilot leads from the people who answer is my call to make, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: My pilot is a €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel that the reservations director signs off on, but the line the respondents see is a generic 'leave your email' put to reservation agents, so the paid, one-hotel shape and who decides are lost.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would your hotel group try this at one hotel for 8 weeks, money back if it doesn't pay? Leave your email and we'll set up a call with your reservations director." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who will ask my questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer and before the last check.
screens.why2: It is plain to me: two named interviewers with a 5-second sample each, a fixed 400-credit cost whichever I pick, and the link going out by text message.
screens.why3: I can judge which voice my reservation agents in Munich and across German hotel groups would take seriously once I have heard each sample.
screens.why4: Two voices are a fair choice, but nothing says whether Daphne or Saskia asks in German, and that matters most to agents at German hotel groups; the hint also says Keel records 'the voice' while the interview is on video with a face.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'reservation agents' and leaks nothing of Codyco or the AI receptionist to the people answering.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ hear 5 s) / Saskia (German, ▶ hear 5 s); Keel records this face and voice once for the project, 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Once I've said who asks my questions, choosing how reservation agents answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Video interviewer, read and tap, or let them choose are plain to me and to anyone who works a desk with a phone and a screen.
screens.why3: I know my agents work between calls on a desk screen or a phone, so I can say how they'd rather answer.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct, cover the real choices (voice, text, both), and my pick 'Read and tap' is there; no escape is needed for a format choice.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco's product or the AI receptionist leaks into the format choice, and it keeps my 'reservation agents' as typed.

screens.why1: After choosing how agents answer, deciding who receives the link is the natural last step before sending.
screens.why2: The first and third options read plainly, but 'the Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's own screen names, and 'signs in with Google' is a detail I'd need to think about for agents at a German hotel group.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm reaching agents I know from our pilot hotels, a list I built, or a group I can post in, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why4: The three channels (named people, a searched list, one open link in a group) are distinct and cover the real ways I'd reach reservation agents, with no escape needed.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or my roles is bent here; it's a plain sending choice, and my pick 'People I know by name' sits as its own option.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (each gets their own link) / A list I found with Keel (Keel makes a link for each, I send them) / A group I post one open link in (each person signs in, then is interviewed)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title, and the deciding count is beside it ('3 beliefs: 3 holding'), with each card giving its own count against its bar (6, 5 and 6 of 7 against 5 of 7).
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on the stage page, but each card says plainly what was counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits ('bar 5 of 7', 'at the bar'), so I read it on first look.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and the adoption line are mine, but the statement is garbled ('the hotel's reservation agent the hotel forwards the call'), it still says calls are handed to the desk 'by rules the hotel sets' when I changed that to the desk taking every handed call, and the relative-advantage line ('would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') is awkward but recognisable.
screens.why_b4: The page never says what three holding beliefs mean for Codyco, for example that the €3,000 pilot ask can go out, or which belief to watch; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: Seven people is a small sample and the page never says so; relative advantage sits exactly on the bar at 5 of 7 yet gets the same 'Holding up' as the others, and 3 of the 6 adoption yeses are conditional but are counted as plain yeses.
screens.instead: Holding up with 7 agents, a small group: forwarding (6 of 7) and handing missed calls to the AI (6 of 7, though 3 had conditions) clear the bar of 5, but 'it would have gone better' only just makes it at 5 of 7. Open that card and the conditions before you ask a hotel group to pay €3,000 for the pilot.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 for against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the forwarding question, the strip shows 7 cells with 6 for and 1 against, and the marker sits at 5. All three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility is my dimension, but I wrote 'could forward unanswered calls to another number'. The card says 'were allowed to have ... forwarded', and the bar line 'You said were allowed to...' puts words in my mouth and doesn't read as a sentence; the stem's 'last booking call' is also not my 'shift with a missed call'.
screens.why_b4: It tells me forwarding won't block me and points me to Adoption friction as the real hurdle, which is a concrete next place to look.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and the count line calls it 'a lean, not a call', but the So line still says flatly that this 'is not what will stop them', and the count line lists the 5 easily and 1 with steps while leaving out the 1 against.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean: 6 of 7 could have had missed calls forwarded (bar 5). The one against, Aylin, has an old phone system only IT can change, so keep a fallback for desks that can't forward, and look at Adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 with the bar at 5 of 7 and says 'at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts better against same or worse over the 7, gives 2 of 7 no difference or worse, and the strip puts the marker at my bar of 5, so I read it at a glance despite the doubled '5 5 a lot'.
screens.why_b3: It is my dimension, and 'missed calls turned into bookings' when a reservation call rang out is my benefit and my problem in my words, though 'one call would have given them missed calls' reads clumsily.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates 5 of 7 and points me to Adoption friction; it does not say that the two against are a group whose call center already covers after six and a sceptic who won't hand guests to a machine, which tells me who to sell to first.
screens.why_b5: It is honest about n ('a lean, not a call', 'at the bar'), but the count line says it was asked about 'their last booking call' when the question was about one that rang out, which misdescribes what the 5 answered.
screens.instead: Held with no margin: 5 of 7, all a lot better, but one more no-difference would sink it. The two against were a group whose call center already covers after hours and a sceptic of AI on the phone, so pitch groups whose calls ring out after six and check Adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over the 7 who answered, and the strip puts the marker at 5 of 7 with the 1-in-3 rule spelled out, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI' are the row I picked, word for word, though the asked clause drops 'that answers in your hotel's name'.
screens.why_b4: The So line says what would make it worth it 'is below', but below is only the same names and the one condition again, with no next step such as proving the forward-to-answer time in the pilot.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the three conditional yeses are split out rather than folded into a clean 6, and 'a lean, not a call' says plainly the group is small.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would hand over missed calls, but 3 only if forwarded calls reach guests without delay: show answer speed on forwarded calls in the pilot. Tobias's No is someone who won't hand guests to an AI at all.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Holding up' and repeats it in the lead line with the deciding count beside it: 'Compatibility held, 6 of 7' against a bar of 5, and 'Relative advantage held, 5 of 7' at a bar of 5.
screens.why_b3: Both dimension names are mine, but the beliefs are reworded: I tested whether they 'could forward unanswered calls to another number', not whether they 'were allowed to', and the Relative advantage line ('would have given them missed calls turned into bookings') is clumsy, though I can still recognise it.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what these two results mean for Codyco, for example that old phone systems need an IT change the owner won't fund, or that groups with an after-hours call center are not my buyer; I have to work that out from the quotes myself.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and 5 of 7 at the bar is not called strong, but Aylin's 'only with help or approval' is presented as 'the 1 who said no', and '1 never saw it (Murat)' sits beside '6 of 7' without saying whether Murat is in the seven.
screens.why_b6: The quotes tell me things I did not type: forwarding can stall on a desk-only phone system and an owner who won't pay to replace it, some guests call precisely to reach a person who knows the house, and where a call center already covers after six, the real pain is group emails without rates.
screens.instead: Compatibility held 6 of 7 (Aylin can forward only once IT changes a phone system the owner won't pay for, so offer to handle that); Relative advantage held exactly at the bar, 5 of 7, and the two against are a group whose call center already covers evenings and a desk that wants guests to reach a person, so lead with groups that have no after-hours cover.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it makes sense to check that I actually work in a hotel group's central reservations office before asking about booking calls.
screens.why2: 'Central reservations office' and 'call centre' are the words we use at work every day, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I work in our group's central reservations office in Munich, so this is simply about my own job.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it completely, and a gate question correctly has no escape option.
screens.why5: It names the segment in the trade's own terms and shows nothing of any product or plan.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question, so I can answer it after hearing it once, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a bit stiff next to the plain 'Yes or no.' the screener's spoken form is supposed to use.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking whether calls went unanswered last week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Reservation call' and 'ring out' are everyday words on our floor, so I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: In our office the ACD queues calls and I see abandoned calls on the wallboard, not a phone I personally 'let' ring, so I'd half-guess whether the abandons in my queue count as mine.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the chips belong to the story box, not the gate.
screens.why5: 'Let ... ring out' adds personal blame the founder's 'not every one gets answered' doesn't carry, so an agent busy on another call during the trade-fair rush may truthfully say No while callers still went unanswered.
screens.why6: One short sentence then 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the problem, unanswered calls, not the routine of taking calls, so a quiet-week agent can say No and a peak-week one Yes, with no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking caller in your queue hang up before anyone picked up? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I let a reservation call ring out this week, it is obvious why I'm now shown something that picks up those calls.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are the words of my desk, and the rest is plain German-office English I follow on first reading.
screens.why3: Unanswered calls, payment, writing bookings into the PMS and handing calls back to the desk are exactly what I deal with on a trade-fair Saturday.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is a deliberate idea card in my own trade's words, with no product jargon or odd role names leaking where they shouldn't, though 'your hotel' sits a little oddly for someone in a group's central office.
screens.why6: Heard once it is long, 'That is OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo' sounds clumsy as its own sentence, and the last line just repeats the first instead of pointing back to the how.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that books the calls nobody picks up. Calls your office misses go to the AI agent. It answers guests in your hotel's voice, takes payment and writes the booking straight into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo. It hands calls to your desk by your own rules. The people building it believe this would turn missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card about booking the calls nobody picks up, it makes sense to ask whether our unanswered calls could be sent somewhere else at all.
screens.why2: Forwarding unanswered calls is everyday phone-system talk in a reservations office, so I understand it on the first hearing.
screens.why3: Whether our phone setup could forward calls is decided by IT or the team lead. Also, my last booking call was answered, so tying it to that call makes me guess about a setting rather than recall something I did.
screens.why4: The four answers cover a permission well: easily, with some steps, only if IT or the supervisor sets it up, or not at all, and 'I can't tell' fits someone who doesn't run the phone system.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own name and line reach me, and the question uses my words, not the founder's product terms.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short answers and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The kind, the passive stem, the four permission answers in order and the escape are all right, but in a central office calls already roll over to colleagues or another queue, so 'another number' is close to settled and almost everyone would say yes; an outside number is what the idea needs.
screens.instead: Think of your last booking call. Could unanswered calls have been forwarded to an outside number or service? Yes, easily · Yes, with some steps · Only with help or approval · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Straight after the idea card and the forwarding question, it's obvious why they now ask whether this AI would have helped on the call that rang out.
screens.why2: The moment is plain to me, but 'helped you turn every guest who calls into a booking better' is a slogan with 'better' dangling at the end; I'd say 'got that caller booked'.
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday calls ring out in our office every hour, so I know that moment and can judge whether something picking it up would have saved the booking.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse is complete and distinct, and 'I can't tell' is the right way out.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, but 'turn every guest who calls into a booking' reads like the company's pitch line rather than how we talk.
screens.why6: Heard once, the stem runs over thirty words, and 'into a booking better, or not' is a mouthful before the four short options, which do say well.
screens.why7: The hard case is the call that went wrong and the job is named, so 'better' has something to point at; there are four fixed options with two for and two against, the belief can be both supported and refuted, and 'I can't tell' is the one escape.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time a reservation call rang out before anyone answered. Would Codyco have helped you get that caller booked? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether it would help, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually let it take my calls; it is the natural last idea question.
screens.why2: I understand 'hand your missed booking calls to it', but 'calls reach guests without delay' is backwards for me, because guests call us, so I would have to read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether missed calls go to an overflow line is set in the telephone system by our team lead or IT, not by me at my headset, so I would partly be guessing for them.
screens.why4: Yes, probably not and no are clear, but the 'Only if' option is garbled; what I would really want is that it books correctly into our reservation system and doesn't sell rooms we don't have on a fair Saturday.
screens.why5: It says plainly what was on the card, an AI that takes the calls nobody picks up, and nothing else of the company's plans or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question with four short options and the escape said last, easy to hold.
screens.why7: The measure and shape are right (Yes, Only if, Probably not, No, then I can't tell apart, with 2 for and 2 against), but routing missed calls is mostly a telephone setup someone else does and sits close to the earlier forwarding question, and the condition does not read as my own assurance.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd let it answer the calls you can't pick up. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it books straight into our system · Probably not · No · I can't tell
